items.title: Proposition 2.7.5: face-structured neighbourhoods

book.label: §2.7.4, Proposition 2.7.5, p. 78 (new in the 2021 edition)
book.statement: In a tame $X$ every $x$ has an open $V$ with $d_X \le d_X(x)$ on $V$, every $y \in V$ in exactly $d_X(y)$ faces of $V$, and an open $U(x) \subseteq V$ such that a face of $V$ meeting $U(x)$ contains $x$.

lean.statement: The same, for every $d$ with the corner axioms; the last property for every open $V \ni x$.

items.title: Definition 2.7.6 and Proposition 2.7.7: the families $N_X$, $N_{X,x}$

book.label: §2.7.4, Definition 2.7.6, p. 79, and Proposition 2.7.7, p. 80 (new in the 2021 edition)
book.statement: An open $V$ is face-structured if every $y \in V$ lies in exactly $d_X(y)$ faces of $V$; $N_X$: the nonempty ones with $d_X|V$ bounded; $N_{X,x}$: those containing $x$ with $d_X \le d_X(x)$. $N_{X,x} \ne \emptyset$; nonempty open subsets and nonempty intersections of members of $N_X$ are in $N_X$; $N_{X,x}$ is closed under intersections.

lean.statement: The same, with $N_X = \bigcup_x N_{X,x}$; every open subset of $[0, \infty)^n \oplus W$ is face-structured.

items.title: Definitions 2.7.8 and 2.7.9: the category $L_X$ and the functor $F_X$

book.label: §2.7.4, Definition 2.7.8, p. 80, and Definition 2.7.9, p. 81 (new in the 2021 edition)
book.statement: Objects $(x, V)$, $x \in \partial X$, $V \in N_{X,x}$; one morphism $(x, V) \to (y, W)$ iff $V \subseteq W$, $x$ lies in $d_X(x)$ faces of $W$ and all contain $y$. $F_X(x, V)$ is the set of faces of $V$ through $x$, and a morphism sends $\theta$ to the face $\theta'$ of $W$ through $x$ and $y$ with $\theta \cap \theta'$ open in $\theta$, an injection (2.43).

lean.statement: The same, $L_X$ as a preorder (thin category), $F_X$ into types, $\theta'$ the union of the faces of $W$ containing $\theta$; morphisms compose, $F_X(\varphi)$ is injective, and bijective over a fixed point.

items.title: Definition 2.7.10: the set $bX$ and the map $B$

book.label: §2.7.4, Definition 2.7.10, p. 81 (new in the 2021 edition)
book.statement: Admissible triples $(x, V, \theta)$, $\theta$ a face of $V \in N_{X,x}$ through $x$; $(x, V, \theta) \sim (x, V', \theta')$ if a smaller $V'' \in N_{X,x}$ has a face sent to $\theta$ and $\theta'$; $bX$ is the set of classes and $B[x, V, \theta] = x$.

lean.statement: The same; $\sim$ is an equivalence relation, $B$ has image $\partial X$, and $B^{-1}(x)$ has exactly $d_X(x)$ points.

items.title: Definition 2.7.11 and (2.44): the sets $U(x, V, \theta)$ and the maps $\Phi$

book.label: §2.7.4, Definition 2.7.11 and (2.44), p. 82 (new in the 2021 edition)
book.statement: $U(x, V, \theta)$: the classes $[y, V', \theta']$ with $y \in \theta$ and a morphism $(y, V') \to (x, V)$ sending $\theta'$ to $\theta$. The canonical bijection $\Phi_{(x, V, \theta)} : U(x, V, \theta) \to \theta$, $[y, V', \theta'] \mapsto y$ (2.44).

lean.statement: $\Phi$ is injective with image $\theta \cap V^x$, $V^x$ the open set of points of $V$ all of whose faces contain $x$; it is a bijection onto $\theta$ if every face of $V$ contains $x$. $V^x$ is such a set and lies in $N_{X,x}$.

items.title: (2.44) for every $V \in N_{X,x}$: an example in $[0, \infty)^3$

items.title: Lemma 2.7.15: the topology $T_{bX}$

book.label: §2.7.4.3, Lemma 2.7.15, p. 85, with the description of $T_{bX}$ before it (new in the 2021 edition)
book.statement: $\mathcal U \in T_{bX}$ if every class in $\mathcal U$ has a representative $(x, V, \theta)$ and a set $O \subseteq \mathcal U \cap U(x, V, \theta)$ with $\Phi_{(x, V, \theta)}(O)$ open in $\theta$; alternatively, a representative with $U(x, V, \theta) \subseteq \mathcal U$. $T_{bX}$ is a topology.

items.title: Proposition 2.7.16: $bX$ is metrizable

book.label: §2.7.4, Proposition 2.7.16, pp. 85–87 (new in the 2021 edition)
book.statement: $T_{bX}$ is metrizable: Hausdorff, locally metrizable through the $\Phi$, and paracompact; Nagata–Smirnov applies.

items.title: Theorem 2.7.13 (topological part) and Definition 2.7.14

items.title: Remark 2.1.6: the modified definition is strictly weaker

items.title: Definition 2.1.16: bundle retractions and bundle maps

book.label: §2.1, Definition 2.1.16 (preprint 2.9), p. 29 (preprint p. 22)
book.statement: An sc-smooth $R(u, v) = (r(u), \rho(u, v))$ on $U \oplus F$, $\rho$ linear in $v$, $R \circ R = R$, is a bundle retraction covering $r$; $\Phi(u, v) = (a(u), \phi(u, v))$, $\phi$ linear in $v$, with \"$p' \circ \Phi = p$\", is a bundle map; $Tr$ is a bundle retraction and $Tf$ a bundle map; the categories $\mathcal R$, $\mathcal{BR}$ and their functors.

items.title: The levels of $X^1$ are those of $X$: $(X^1)_m \cong X_{m+1}$

items.title: Theorem 2.3.16: $p : TX \to X^1$ as an sc-smooth bundle

book.statement: A construction associating to an M-polyfold $X$ the sc-smooth M-polyfold bundle $p : TX \to X^1$, locally built on the bundle retractions $TO \to O^1$ with sc-smooth bundle maps as transition maps.

items.title: Proposition 2.3.17 for $i = 1$: $T(X^1) \equiv (TX)^1$

book.statement: $(TX)^i$ and $T(X^i)$ are naturally identified, also as bundles $(TX)^i \to (X^1)^i$ and $T(X^i) \to (X^i)^1$, covering $(X^1)^i \equiv (X^i)^1$.

items.title: Definition 3.1.1 (preprint 3.1): sc-germs of neighbourhoods

book.label: §3.1, Definition 3.1.1 (preprint 3.1), p. 89 (preprint p. 62)
book.statement: An sc-germ of neighbourhoods $\mathcal O(C, 0)$ around $0$ in a partial quadrant $C \subseteq E$ is a decreasing sequence $U_0 \supset U_1 \supset \cdots$ with $U_m$ a relatively open neighbourhood of $0$ in $C_m = C \cap E_m$; its tangent $T\mathcal O(C, 0)$ is $U_1 \oplus E_0 \supset U_2 \oplus E_1 \supset \cdots$. A relatively open $U \ni 0$ with $U_m = U \cap E_m$ is an example; \"the size of the sets $U_m$ does not matter\".

lean.statement: An `ScNbhdGerm E C` is a family of sets $U_m \subseteq E_m$, each of the form $O \cap C_m$ with $O$ open and $0 \in U_m$, nested along the inclusions $E_{m+1} \to E_m$. Its tangent germ has levels $U_{m+1} \times E_m$; `ofSet` is the text's example $U_m = U \cap E_m$. The theorems on germs ask $C$ to be *quadrant-like* (every $C_m$ convex with nonempty interior, $0 \in C$), which every partial quadrant is; then derivatives on $U_1$ are unique.

chips: a germ is a fixed sequence of sets
diff: A germ is a fixed sequence of sets, not a class \"up to shrinking\". The text's remark that the size of the $U_m$ does not matter is therefore not built in; where it matters (Theorems 3.3.3, 3.3.6, Corollary 3.3.7 (preprint Theorems 3.30, 3.33, 3.34) and Theorem 3.35 (preprint; not in the 2021 edition)) the formal statements say on which germ they hold (V3.27, V3.30–V3.32).

The re-indexed sequence $(U_{m+1})_m$ is a germ only when all levels coincide (a finite-dimensional parameter space); the text does not remark this, and the germ implicit function theorem uses it once per derivative.

items.title: Definition 3.1.2 (preprint 3.2): sc$^k$-germs

book.label: §3.1, Definition 3.1.2 (preprint 3.2), pp. 90–91 (preprint pp. 62–63)
book.statement: An sc$^0$-germ $f : \mathcal O(C, 0) \to F$ is a continuous $f : U_0 \to F$ with $f(U_m) \subseteq F_m$ and $f : U_m \to F_m$ continuous. It is sc$^1$ if for $x \in U_1$ there is a bounded $Df(x) : E_0 \to F_0$ with $|f(x + h) - f(x) - Df(x)h|_0 / |h|_1 \to 0$ ($h \in E_1$, $x + h \in U_1$) and $Tf(x, h) = (f(x), Df(x)h)$ is an sc$^0$-germ on $T\mathcal O(C, 0)$; sc$^k$ inductively, sc-smooth if sc$^k$ for all $k$.

lean.statement: `IsSc0Germ`, `IsSc1GermWith` (with a given derivative family), `IsSc1Germ`, `IsSckGerm`, `IsScSmoothGerm` are the notions of Definitions 1.1.13–1.1.15 and of the unnumbered definition after them (preprint Definitions 1.12–1.15) with $U \cap E_m$ replaced by $U_m$. An sc$^k$ map on a relatively open $U \ni 0$ is an sc$^k$-germ on `ofSet U`.

diff: As in the text, with the derivative family chosen (as in Chapter 1); it is unique on $U_1$ for quadrant-like $C$ (`IsSc1GermWith.eq_of_uniqueDiffWithinAt`).

items.title: The calculus of germs

book.label: §3.1–§3.3, used without statement (proofs of Lemma 3.3.4 (preprint 3.31), Theorems 3.3.6, 3.4.2 (preprint 3.33, 3.38)), preprint p. 62
book.statement: Not stated: the text restricts, composes and pairs germs and applies sc-operators to them as it does with maps on open sets.

lean.statement: (1) sc$^k$-germs depend only on the values on $U_0$ and restrict to smaller germs; (2) the chain rule: if $f$ is an sc$^k$-germ on $G$, $g$ an sc$^k$-germ on $G'$ and $f$ maps $U_m$ into $U'_m$ for every $m$, then $g \circ f$ is an sc$^k$-germ and $T(g \circ f) = Tg \circ Tf$ on $TG$; (3) sc-operators are sc-smooth germs on every germ; (4) the pairing of two sc$^k$-germs is an sc$^k$-germ; (5) the germ $\{x \in G_0 : f(x) \in G'\}$ on which an sc$^0$-germ maps into a given germ.

diff: The chain rule needs the inner germ to map $U_m$ into the domain $U'_m$ of the outer one on every level (`ScNbhdGerm.MapsToGerm`); for maps on open sets this is $f(U) \subseteq V$. The shrinking of germs that the text performs with \"near $0$\" is `ScNbhdGerm.preimage`.

items.title: Propositions 1.2.1–1.2.3 (preprint 1.16–1.18) for germs

book.label: §3.1, proof of Lemma 3.1.9 (preprint 3.9) ("recalling Proposition 1.17"), Lemma 3.3.4 (preprint 3.31), Corollary 3.3.7 (preprint 3.34), preprint p. 67
book.statement: Not stated: Propositions 1.2.1–1.2.3 (preprint 1.16–1.18) are stated in Chapter 1 for relatively open sets; the proofs of Lemma 3.1.9 (preprint 3.9), Lemma 3.3.4 (preprint 3.31) and Corollary 3.3.7 (preprint 3.34) apply them to germs.

lean.statement: For an sc$^1$-germ $f$ with derivative family $D$: $Df(x)$, $x \in U_{m+1}$, restricts to bounded level operators $E_m \to F_m$, jointly continuous in $(x, h)$ (also in operator norm), and $f : U_{m+1} \to F_m$ is differentiable within $U_{m+1}$ with these derivatives (1.16); the shifted sequence $(U_{m+1})_m$ is a germ in $E^1$ and an sc$^k$-germ on $G$ is an sc$^k$-germ $G^1 \to F^1$ (1.17); an sc$^k$-germ is $C^k$ from $U_{m+k}$ to $F_m$ (1.18).

diff: The proofs are those of Chapter 1 with $U \cap E_m$ replaced by $U_m$. The text's \"recalling Proposition 1.17\" in Lemma 3.1.9 (preprint 3.9) is Proposition 1.2.1 (preprint 1.16) for germs.

items.title: Definition 3.1.3 (preprint 3.3): sc-smooth section germs

book.label: §3.1, Definition 3.1.3 (preprint 3.3), p. 91 (preprint p. 63)
book.statement: An sc-smooth section germ $(f, x_0)$ of $P : Y \to X$ is a continuous section $f : V \to P^{-1}(V)$ near the smooth point $x_0$ such that in a strong bundle chart with $\varphi(x_0) = 0$ the principal part $\mathbf f$ of $\Phi \circ f \circ \varphi^{-1} : O \to K$ has $\mathbf f \circ r : \mathcal O(C, 0) \to F$ an sc-smooth germ.

lean.statement: `StrongBundle.IsScSmoothSectionGerm f x₀`: $x_0$ smooth, and for some strong bundle chart compatible with the atlas (`StrongBundle.IsChart`) with $\varphi(x_0) = 0$, $\mathbf f \circ r$ is an sc-smooth germ on some sc-germ of neighbourhoods $G$ with $G_0 \subseteq U$, whose levels may shrink with $m$ (the text’s germ reading). An sc-smooth section is an sc-smooth section germ at every smooth point with a centred chart (with the germ $U \cap E_m$).

diff: \"A strong bundle chart\" is read as a chart compatible with the atlas, not a member of it: a chart of the atlas need not be centred at $x_0$, and the notion must not depend on the atlas within its class (Findings, Chapter 3, item 41). That it does not is proved: equivalent atlases have the same compatible charts (`isChart_congr`; V2.58, Findings, Chapter 2, item 43). Updated in the third addendum of this page.
Continuity of $f$ near $x_0$ is not a separate field: it follows near $x_0$ from the continuity of $\mathbf f \circ r$ on level $0$ of the germ.

**Germs.** Since the fourth addendum of this page the definition is in the text’s germ reading: $\mathbf f \circ r$ is an sc-smooth germ on some sc-germ of neighbourhoods inside $U$, whose levels may shrink with $m$, as for Definitions 3.1.4, 3.1.6 and 3.1.11 (preprint 3.4, 3.6 and 3.11) since phase 2. Before, it was required on the whole $U$ of the chart (levels $U \cap E_m$), which is stricter: a function $C^k$ on $(-1/k, 1/k)$ for every $k$ is an sc-smooth germ in the constant scale $\mathbb R$ and sc-smooth on no neighbourhood of $0$ (`exists_isScSmoothGerm_not_isScSmooth`). No theorem assumes the definition. Hence “hypotheses explicit” again (“narrower” from the third addendum until the fourth) (Findings, Chapter 3, items 220–221, 260; round-trip item V3.5).

items.title: The section algebra and the sum rule

book.label: §3.1, used in Theorems 3.1.13, 3.1.18 (preprint 3.12, 3.15) ("$f + s$ is an sc-smooth section"), p. 98 (preprint p. 71)
book.statement: Not stated: the fibrewise sum of sections, principal parts in a chart, the sum rule of the sc-calculus, and the sc-smoothness of the local representatives of sc$^+$-sections in a chart that is not in the atlas.

lean.statement: The fibrewise sum $f + s$ is a section with principal part $\mathbf f + \mathbf s$ in every chart; $f(x) = 0$ iff $\mathbf f(\varphi(x)) = 0$; the fibres of $K$ are linear. Sums, differences and negatives of sc-smooth maps on relatively open subsets of partial quadrants are sc-smooth. In every strong bundle chart compatible with the atlas, $z \mapsto (z, \mathbf f(z))$ is sc-smooth $O \to K$ for an sc-smooth section and $z \mapsto (z, \mathbf s_1(z))$ is sc-smooth $O \to K[1]$ for an sc$^+$-section.

diff: For an sc$^+$-section in a chart outside the atlas the sc-smoothness of the representative is the change of chart $(\Phi \circ \Phi'^{-1})[1]$, i.e. the compatibility on $[1]$ of Definition 2.6.4 (preprint 2.50); this is its first use (Findings, Chapter 3, item 41).
The sum rule is pairing followed by the sc-operator $F \oplus F \to F$.

items.title: Definition 3.1.4 (preprint 3.4): fillers

book.label: §3.1, Definition 3.1.4 (preprint 3.4), p. 91 (preprint p. 64)
book.statement: For a tame strong local bundle $K = R(U \triangleleft F) \to O$, $R(u, h) = (r(u), \rho(u)h)$, $r(0) = 0$, an sc-smooth section germ $(f, 0)$ has a filling $(g, 0)$ (an sc-smooth section germ of $U \triangleleft F \to U$) if (1) $f = g$ on $O$ near $0$; (2) $g(y) = \rho(r(y))g(y)$ for $y \in U$ near $0$ forces $y \in O$; (3) the linearization of $y \mapsto [1 - \rho(r(y))]g(y)$ at $0$, restricted to $\ker Dr(0)$, is a topological isomorphism onto $\ker\rho(0)$.

lean.statement: `IsFillingGerm` for the principal parts $f, g : E_0 \to F_0$ (the text’s germ reading, also Definition 3.1.6 (preprint 3.6), V3.9): $g$ is an sc-smooth germ on an sc-germ of neighbourhoods $G$ with $G_0 \subseteq U$; (1) and (2) near $0$; (3) the map $y \mapsto [1 - \rho(r(y))]g(y)$ (`fillDefect`) is an sc$^1$-germ on $G$ with a derivative family $Dk$, and $Dk(0)$ induces a continuous linear equivalence $\ker Dr(0) \simeq \ker\rho(0)$. Here $r(u) = (R(u, 0))_1$, $\rho(u)h = (R(u, h))_2$, with $R(u, h) = (r(u), \rho(u)h)$, $r \circ r = r$, $\rho(x)$ a projection for $x \in O$, and $\rho(u)$ a bounded operator. The whole-chart form `IsFillerOf` asks the map in (3) to be sc$^1$ on all of $U$ and says nothing about the regularity of $g$.

chips: sc¹ of the map in (3) required
diff: Condition (3) presupposes that $y \mapsto [1 - \rho(r(y))]g(y)$ is differentiable at $0$; it is required to be an sc$^1$-germ with a derivative family, which holds for every sc-smooth germ $g$ (`fillDefect_isScSmoothGerm`); the value of the family at $0$ is unique (Findings, Chapter 3, items 261, 272).
The sc-smoothness of $g$ is part of the filling, as in the text (“$(g, 0)$ an sc-smooth section germ”); tameness of the retraction is not used.

**Germs.** Since the switch to the text’s germ reading (phase 2) $g$ and the map in (3) are germs whose levels may shrink with $m$ (`IsFillingGerm`); the stricter whole-chart filler (`IsFillerOf`, with $g$ sc-smooth on all of $U$ added in `IsFilledVersion`) is kept for the `…WholeChart` notions. Hence “hypotheses explicit” again (“narrower” in the third addendum) (Findings, Chapter 3, items 220–221, 261, 330; round-trip items V3.7, V3.19). On the text’s domain of definition, tame strong local bundles, it is not broader: tameness is simply not used.

items.title: Proposition 3.1.5 (preprint 3.5): the filler and the linearization

book.label: §3.1, the paragraph after Definition 3.1.4 (preprint 3.4) and Proposition 3.1.5 (preprint 3.5), pp. 91–93 (preprint pp. 64–65)
book.statement: If $f$ has the filling $g$ and $f(0) = 0$, then in the splittings $E = Dr(0)E \oplus \ker Dr(0)$, $F = \rho(0)F \oplus \ker\rho(0)$, $Dg(0) = \begin{pmatrix} Tf(0) & * \\ 0 & C \end{pmatrix}$ with $C$ an isomorphism, and (1) $Tf(0) : Dr(0)E \to \rho(0)F$ is onto iff $Dg(0)$ is; (2) $Tf(0)$ is Fredholm iff $Dg(0)$ is, with equal index.

lean.statement: For a filler $g$ of $f$ with $g$ sc-smooth, $g(0) = 0$ and $f$ a section of $K \to O$: $D(\rho(r(\cdot))g)(0) = \rho(0)Dg(0)$, $(1 - \rho(0))Dg(0)Dr(0) = 0$, $D(f \circ r)(0) = Dg(0)Dr(0)$; and $Tf(0) := Dg(0)|_{Dr(0)E} : Dr(0)E \to \rho(0)F$ is onto iff $Dg(0)$ is, Fredholm iff $Dg(0)$ is, and $\mathrm{ind}\,Tf(0) = \mathrm{ind}\,Dg(0)$. The linear algebra holds for any idempotents $p, q$ and $L$ with $(1 - q)Lp = 0$ and $(1 - q)L : \ker p \to \ker q$ a topological isomorphism. In sc form: if $Dg(0)$ is an sc-Fredholm sc-operator, then $Dr(0)E$, $\rho(0)F$, $\ker Dr(0)$ and $\ker\rho(0)$ are sc-subspaces, $Tf(0) : Dr(0)E \to \rho(0)F$ is sc-Fredholm, of index $\mathrm{ind}\,Dg(0)$ on every level, and $(1 - \rho(0))Dg(0) : \ker Dr(0) \to \ker\rho(0)$ is an sc-isomorphism (condition (3) of the filler on every level). Conversely, for $Dg(0)$ an sc-operator: $Dg(0)$ is sc-Fredholm if and only if $Tf(0)$ is sc-Fredholm and condition (3) holds on every level. The same for a filling germ (V3.7), with $Dg(0)$ the value at $0$ of any derivative family of $g$ on any germ (`IsFillingGerm.proposition_3_5`, `IsFillingGerm.proposition_3_5_sc`, `IsFillingGerm.proposition_3_5_sc_iff`).

chips: sc form: filler (3) on level 0 suffices
sc converse needs (3) on every level
diff: The proof exhibits $\ker Tf(0) \simeq \ker Dg(0)$ and $\mathrm{coker}\,Tf(0) \simeq \mathrm{coker}\,Dg(0)$ directly instead of the text's factorization and additivity of the index, so the index equality holds as $\dim\ker - \dim\mathrm{coker}$ with no finiteness assumption; closedness of the ranges transfers through the continuous $y \mapsto y - LC^{-1}(1 - q)y$, which is where \"topological\" in (3) is used.
The text's \"by linearization at $y = 0$\" needs $(u, h) \mapsto \rho(u)h$ differentiable and $g(0) = 0$; the target \"$(1 - D\rho(0))F$\" is $(1 - \rho(0))F$ (Findings, Chapter 3, item 47).

Proposition 3.1.5 (2) (preprint 3.5) is a level-$0$ statement. Its sc form in the direction Proposition 3.6.5 (preprint 3.52) uses (“$Dg(0)$ sc-Fredholm ⟹ $Tf(0)$ sc-Fredholm”) needs condition (3) of the filler on level $0$ only, as the text states it: the higher levels of $Tf(0)$ come from the regularity of $Dg(0)$ (`IsScFredholm.restrict`), and condition (3) on every level then follows at the zero. The converse in sc form needs condition (3) on every level as a hypothesis; with level $0$ only it fails (an example on a weighted $\ell^2$ with the shift, Findings, Chapter 3, item 238, not formalized). Nothing in the text uses the converse (Findings, Chapter 3, items 234, 237, 238). Updated in the third addendum of this page.

For filling germs (the text’s reading of Definition 3.1.4 (preprint 3.4)) the proofs are the same, with the derivative family of the fill defect in place of the derivative on $U$ (Findings, Chapter 3, items 272, 289, 314). Updated after the switch of Definition 3.1.11 (preprint 3.11) to the text’s germ reading (phase 2).

items.title: Definition 3.1.6 (preprint 3.6): filled versions

book.label: §3.1, Definition 3.1.6 (preprint 3.6), p. 93 (preprint p. 66)
book.statement: $(f, x_0)$ has a filling if in a strong bundle chart with $\varphi(x_0) = 0$ the section germ $\Phi \circ f \circ \varphi^{-1} : O \to K$ has a filling $g : U \to U \triangleleft F$ near $0$; $(g, 0)$ is a filled version.

lean.statement: `IsFillingGerm fb g` (V3.7): $g$ is an sc-smooth germ on an sc-germ of neighbourhoods $G$, $G_0 \subseteq U$, whose levels may shrink with $m$, and fills the principal part $\mathbf f$ near $0$; the centred chart is that of Definition 3.1.11 (preprint 3.11) (V3.13). The whole-chart form `IsFilledVersion` ($g$ sc-smooth on all of $U$, filling in the sense of `IsFillerOf`) is a filling (`IsFilledVersion.isFillingGerm`), and a filling sc-smooth on all of $U$ is a filled version (`IsFillingGerm.isFilledVersion`).

chips: local data; the chart in Def. 3.1.11
diff: The text asks for a filling of the section germ in some strong bundle chart centred at $x_0$; the formal notion is the datum in a given chart, for the principal parts, and the centred chart is quantified in Definition 3.1.11 (preprint 3.11) (V3.13).

**Germs.** Since the switch to the text’s germ reading (phase 2) the filling is a germ (`IsFillingGerm`). The earlier filled version, sc-smooth on all of $U$, is stricter (round-trip items V3.9, V3.43) and is kept as `IsFilledVersion`, exactly the fillings sc-smooth on $U$. Hence “restated” again (“narrower” in the third addendum) (Findings, Chapter 3, items 220–221, 260–262, 330).

items.title: Definition 3.1.7 (preprint 3.7): basic germs

book.label: §3.1, Definition 3.1.7 (preprint 3.7), p. 94 (preprint p. 66)
book.statement: A basic germ is an sc-smooth germ $f : \mathcal O([0, \infty)^k \oplus \mathbb R^{n-k} \oplus W, 0) \to \mathbb R^N \oplus W$ with $f(0) = 0$ and $P_W \circ f(a, w) = w - B(a, w)$, $B(0, 0) = 0$, $|B(a, w) - B(a, w')|_m \le \varepsilon|w - w'|_m$ for $(a, w), (a, w')$ close enough to $(0, 0)$ on level $m$, for every $\varepsilon > 0$, $m \ge 0$.

lean.statement: `IsBasicGerm C̃ G f B`: $f$ an sc-smooth germ on the germ $G$ around $0$ in $\widetilde C \oplus W$ with $f(0) = 0$, whose $W$-component is $w - B(a, w)$ on $U_0$, with $B$ an sc$^0$-contraction germ (V3.25: $B$ sc$^0$, $B(0, 0) = 0$, and the contraction estimate on balls whose points lie in $U_m$). $\widetilde C$ is a quadrant-like subset of a finite-dimensional $P$, $\mathbb R^N$ any finite-dimensional $Q$.

chips: points of the balls lie in $U_m$
diff: \"Close enough on level $m$\" presupposes that the points lie in the domain $U_m$; this is required. The theorems that use basic germs add \"$\widetilde C$ closed\" or \"a partial quadrant\" where needed.
Remark 3.1.8 (preprint 3.8) (in [21] $f(0) = 0$ was not required) is a historical remark and makes no claim.

items.title: Lemma 3.1.9 (preprint 3.9): the fibre derivative of $B$ is small

book.label: §3.1, Lemma 3.1.9 (preprint 3.9), p. 94 (preprint p. 67)
book.statement: For $B$ as in Definition 3.1.7 (preprint 3.7), every $\varepsilon > 0$ and $m \ge 0$: $|D_2B(a, w)\zeta|_m \le \varepsilon|\zeta|_m$ for $\zeta \in W_m$ if $(a, w) \in E_{m+1}$ is close enough to $(0, 0)$ in $E_m$; in particular $D_2B(0, 0) = 0$.

lean.statement: Four formal forms: (a) on level $m$, for an sc$^1$-germ $B$ in the working form of a contraction germ, $\|D_2B(a, w)\|_{L(W_m)} \le \tfrac12$ at points $(a, w) \in U_{m+1}$ with $a \in N(m+1)$, $w \in O(m+1)$, $\iota w \in O(m)$; (b) $D_2B(0, 0) = 0$ for an sc$^1$ sc$^0$-contraction germ; (c) on level $0$ with arbitrary $\varepsilon$: $|D_2B(x)\zeta|_0 \le \varepsilon|\zeta|_0$ for $x \in U_1$ small on level $1$. (d) **as stated**: for $B$ an sc$^1$ sc$^0$-contraction germ on a quadrant-like $\widetilde C$, for every $\varepsilon > 0$ and every $m$ there is $r > 0$ with $|D_2B(x)\zeta|_m \le \varepsilon|\zeta|_m$ for $\zeta \in W_m$ at every $x \in U_{m+1}$ with $|x|_m < r$.

diff: Stronger in regularity: $B$ sc$^1$ suffices (Theorem 3.3.3 (preprint 3.30) and Lemma 3.3.4 (preprint 3.31) apply the lemma to sc$^1$ and sc$^k$ germs).

The general statement (every $\varepsilon$, every level $m$, points of $E_{m+1}$ small in $E_m$) is proved as stated, from the contraction estimate of Definition 3.3.1 (preprint 3.28) applied at points small on level $0$; smallness on level $m + 1$ is not needed (Findings, Chapter 3, item 215). It is what Proposition 3.1.10 (preprint 3.10) on level $m$ (V3.12) and Lemma 3.3.4 (preprint 3.31) in the sense of Definition 3.3.1 (preprint 3.28) (V3.28) use. The constant $\tfrac12$ on level $m$ in the working form, the value at $(0, 0)$ and the level-$0$ form are kept for the theorems that use them. Formerly narrower (the general statement not formalized). Updated in the third addendum of this page.

items.title: Proposition 3.1.10 (preprint 3.10): the linearization of a basic germ plus an sc$^+$-germ

book.label: §3.1, Proposition 3.1.10 (preprint 3.10), p. 95 (preprint p. 68)
book.statement: If $f = h + s$ with $h$ a basic germ and $s$ an sc$^+$-germ, $f(0) = 0$, then $Df(0) : \mathbb R^n \oplus W \to \mathbb R^N \oplus W$ is sc-Fredholm of index $n - N$; and for every $m$, $Df(a, w)$ on level $m$ is Fredholm of index $n - N$ for $(a, w) \in E_{m+1}$ small in $E_m$.

lean.statement: For a basic germ $h$, an $s$ sc$^1$ into $(\mathbb R^N \oplus W)^1$ and $f = h + s$ sc$^1$: $Df(0)$ is an sc-operator, sc-Fredholm of index $\dim P - \dim Q$; it is $T_0 + S$ with $T_0(\delta a, \delta w) = (0, \delta w)$ (sc-Fredholm of index $n - N$) and an sc$^+$-operator $S$ built level by level. For the data of Theorem 3.4.2 (preprint 3.38) and $x \in U_1$ small on level $1$, $D(h + s)(x) : E_0 \to F_0$ is Fredholm of index $n - N$. **On every level** (the second statement): for every $m$ there is $\delta > 0$ such that at every $x \in U_{m+1}$ with $|x|_m < \delta$ the level-$m$ operator $Df(x)_m : \mathbb R^n \oplus W_m \to \mathbb R^N \oplus W_m$ is Fredholm of index $\dim P - \dim Q$, for $\widetilde C$ quadrant-like (partial quadrants are); $f(0) = 0$ is not used.

diff: First statement as in the text, with $s$ only sc$^1$ into $F^1$ and $f$ only sc$^1$. The verification that $Df(0) - T_0$ is sc$^+$ (finite-rank terms through $\mathbb R^n$ and $\mathbb R^N$ with smooth values because $Dh(0)$ is an sc-operator at the smooth point $0$) is not in the text (Findings, Chapter 3, item 46).

Second statement: on every level $m$, at the points of $U_{m+1}$ small in $E_m$, as in the text, by the text's proof: $Df(x)_m = T_0 + S(x) + K(x)$ with $\|S(x)\| \le \varepsilon$ by Lemma 3.1.9 (preprint 3.9) on level $m$ (V3.11) and $K(x)$ compact (finite rank, and $\iota\,\mathrm{pr}_W Ds(x)$ through $W_{m+1} \to W_m$). The one identity the text uses silently, the $W$-component of $Df(x)_m$, is proved from the uniqueness of derivatives within $U_1$ (Findings, Chapter 3, item 230). With both statements as in the text under weaker hypotheses ($s$ and $f$ only sc$^1$, $f(0) = 0$ unused) the verdict is “stronger”; formerly narrower, the second statement on level $0$ only (G.21). Updated in the third addendum of this page.

items.title: Definition 3.1.11 (preprint 3.11): sc-Fredholm germs

book.label: §3.1, Definition 3.1.11 (preprint 3.11), p. 96 (preprint p. 69)
book.statement: $(f, x_0)$ is an sc-Fredholm germ if it has a filled version $(g, 0)$ and a local sc$^+$-section $s$ with $s(0) = g(0)$ such that $g - s$ is conjugated to a basic germ: a strong bundle isomorphism $\Psi : U \triangleleft F \to U' \triangleleft F'$ covering an sc-diffeomorphism $\psi$ with $\Psi \circ (g - s) \circ \psi^{-1}$ a basic germ.

lean.statement: `StrongBundle.IsScFredholmGerm f x₀` (the text’s germ reading): in a strong bundle chart of $P$ centred at $x_0$, a filling $g$ (`IsFillingGerm`, an sc-smooth germ on a germ of neighbourhoods inside $U$, V3.9), a local sc$^+$-section $s$ (`IsScPlusGerm`: $s : E_0 \to F_1$ an sc-smooth germ into $F^1$ on a germ inside $U$) with $\iota s(0) = g(0)$, and `IsConjugateToBasicGerm` for $u \mapsto g(u) - \iota s(u)$: strong bundle maps $\Psi, \Psi'$ inverse to each other (`IsStrongBundleIso`), $\psi(0) = 0$, $U'$ relatively open in $\widetilde C \oplus W$ ($\widetilde C$ a partial quadrant of a finite-dimensional space), a basic germ $h$ on a germ inside $U'$, and $(\Psi(u, g(u) - s(u)))_2 = h(\psi(u))$ for $u \in U$ near $0$.

diff: The conjugation identity is required for $u \in U$ near $0$ (Theorem 3.1.18's (preprint 3.15) identity $(g + \tilde t) - (\tilde t + t_0) = g - t_0$ holds on $U$ only). The text's $C' = T\psi(0)C$ (used in Theorem 3.6.8 (preprint 3.54)) is not part of the data; it is proved (V3.48).
The index statement after the definition is V3.46 (Proposition 3.6.5 (preprint 3.52), in the chart).
The witnesses of the conjugation are also available as a structure, `ConjugationData`, so that the dimensions of the basic germ can be named (V3.46).

**Germs.** Since the switch to the text’s germ reading (phase 2) the filling and the sc$^+$-section are germs whose levels may shrink with $m$; $\Psi$ is a strong bundle isomorphism on all of $U$, which is no restriction (on a relatively open $U_0 \subseteq U$ it is the same after restricting the chart on level $0$). The project’s earlier notion, with $g$ and $s$ sc-smooth on the whole $U$, is `IsScFredholmGermWholeChart`: it implies the germ reading and is exactly the germ reading with $g$, $s$ sc-smooth on $U$ (`isScFredholmGerm_iff_germG_wholeChart`). Whether the two agree for sections sc-smooth on $X$ is open, and no theorem depends on it (Findings, Chapter 3, items 220–221, 261–264, 330). What remains is the formulation above and the untamed chart (formerly also the stricter germ side, third addendum).

The existential over charts is essential: a filling in a chart gives a topological isomorphism $\ker Dr(0) \cong \ker\rho(0)$ (`IsFillingGerm.nonempty_kerEquiv`), a condition on the chart, so a filling in one chart gives none in another unless these normal spaces match; a compatible tame chart of the trivial bundle carries no filling of any section (`TrivialBundle.not_isFillingGerm_evenBundleChart`) (Findings, Chapter 3, items 350–352). Added in the fourth addendum of this page.

items.title: Theorem 3.1.13 (preprint 3.12): local compactness for sc-Fredholm germs

book.label: §3.1, Theorem 3.1.13 (preprint 3.12), p. 97 (preprint p. 70) ("an immediate consequence of Theorem 3.40")
book.statement: Let $f$ be an sc-smooth section of the tame strong bundle $P : Y \to X$ and $(f, x_0)$ an sc-Fredholm germ with $f(x_0) = 0$. There are nested open neighbourhoods $O(0) \supset O(1) \supset \cdots$ of $x_0$ in $X_0$ such that $\mathrm{cl}_{X_0}\{x \in O(i) \mid f(x) = 0\}$ is a compact subset of $X_i$.

lean.statement: For a section $f$ ($P \circ f = \mathrm{id}$) of any strong bundle with $(f, x_0)$ an sc-Fredholm germ and $f(x_0) = 0$: nested open $O(i) \ni x_0$ such that the closure in $X$ of $\{x \in O(i) \mid f(x) = 0\}$ is the image of a compact subset of $X_i$ (level topology) under the inclusion $X_i \to X$.

diff: Of \"$f$ an sc-smooth section of the tame strong bundle\" only $P \circ f = \mathrm{id}$ is used; regularity enters through the filling germ (germ reading, V3.13); tameness not at all.

\"Immediate consequence of Theorem 3.40\" hides: the correspondence of zeros through chart, filler and the fibre maps of $\Psi$; the push-forward $t$ of the sc$^+$-section is an sc$^+$-germ with $t(0) = 0$; shrinking so that $E_0$-closures stay inside the chart and the region of the identities; and the continuity of the inverse chart $O_i \to X_i$ for the level topology (Findings, Chapter 3, items 12, 44).

items.title: Corollary 3.1.15 (preprint 3.13): convergence on every level

book.label: §3.1, Corollary 3.1.15 (preprint 3.13), p. 97 (preprint p. 70)
book.statement: Under the hypotheses of Theorem 3.1.13 (preprint 3.12), if $f(x_k) = 0$ and $x_k \to x$ in $X_0$, then for every $m$, $x_k \in X_m$ for $k$ large and $x_k \to x$ in $X_m$.

lean.statement: (a) If $f(x_k) = 0$ and $x_k \to x_0$ (the base point of the germ), then for every $m$ there are lifts $y_k \in X_m$ of the $x_k$, $k$ large, converging in $X_m$ to the lift of $x_0$. (b) For an sc-Fredholm section and any limit $x$ of zeros: $x$ is a zero and a smooth point, and the same conclusion holds at $x$.

chips: limit $x_0$, or any limit for sections
diff: As stated, the corollary concerns an arbitrary limit $x$ while the hypothesis is about the germ at $x_0$; it is proved for $x = x_0$, and for any limit when $f$ is an sc-Fredholm section, which provides the germ property at $x$ (Findings, Chapter 3, items 15, 45).
$X_m$ is not known to be first countable here, so convergence is proved by a cluster-point argument in the compact set of Theorem 3.1.13 (preprint 3.12).

items.title: Definition 3.1.16 (preprint 3.14): sc-Fredholm sections

book.label: §3.1, Definition 3.1.16 (preprint 3.14), p. 97 (preprint p. 70)
book.statement: A section $f$ of the tame strong bundle $P : Y \to X$ is sc-Fredholm if (1) it is sc-smooth; (2) regularizing: $x \in X_m$, $f(x) \in Y_{m,m+1}$ imply $x \in X_{m+1}$; (3) $(f, x)$ is an sc-Fredholm germ at every smooth point $x$.

lean.statement: `StrongBundle.IsScFredholmSection f`: (1)–(3) for a section of any strong bundle, clause (3) in the germ reading of V3.13. A zero of a regularizing section is a smooth point.

diff: As in the text; the bundle is not required to be tame, which plays no role in the definition (Findings, Chapter 3, item 40).

**Germs.** Clause (3) is the germ notion of V3.13, the text’s germ reading since the switch (phase 2); the earlier whole-chart notion, stricter, is `IsScFredholmSectionWholeChart` and implies this one (`IsScFredholmSectionWholeChart.isScFredholmSection`). Hence “as in the book” again (“restated” in the third addendum) (Findings, Chapter 3, items 220–221, 330).

items.title: Theorem 3.1.18 (preprint 3.15): stability under sc$^+$-perturbations

book.label: §3.1, Theorem 3.1.18 (preprint 3.15), p. 98 (preprint p. 71) (proof preprint pp. 72–73)
book.statement: If $P : Y \to X$ is a strong bundle over a tame M-polyfold, $f \in \mathrm{Fred}(P)$ and $s \in \Gamma^+(P)$, then $f + s \in \mathrm{Fred}(P)$.

lean.statement: For any strong bundle: if $f$ is an sc-Fredholm section and $s$ an sc$^+$-section, the fibrewise sum $f + s$ is an sc-Fredholm section: sc-smooth (sum rule in the charts), regularizing ($Y_{m,m+1}$ is closed under fibrewise subtraction and $s$ takes values in $Y_{m,m+1}$ over $X_m$), and an sc-Fredholm germ at every smooth point (filling germ $g + \tilde t$ on the germ of $g$, sc$^+$-germ $\tilde t + t_0$ on the germ of $t_0$, the same conjugation).

diff: Tameness is not used (Findings, Chapter 3, item 40).
The text's \"$f + s$ is an sc-smooth section which is also regularizing\" is two proofs here (Findings, Chapter 3, item 42).

In the germ reading of Definition 3.1.11 (preprint 3.11) (V3.13), with the text’s proof: $\tilde t = \hat s \circ r$ is sc-smooth on the whole $U$ because $s$ is a global sc$^+$-section, and a germ plus a whole-chart map is a germ on the same germ (Lemma 3.1.20 (preprint 3.17) for germs, V3.19); the whole-chart form is `theorem_3_15_wholeChart` (Findings, Chapter 3, item 300). Updated after the switch of Definition 3.1.11 (preprint 3.11) to the text’s germ reading (phase 2).

items.title: Lemma 3.1.19 (preprint 3.16): the extension $\tilde s = s \circ r$

book.label: §3.1, Lemma 3.1.19 (preprint 3.16), p. 99 (preprint p. 72)
book.statement: An sc$^+$-section $s : O \to K$ extends to the sc$^+$-section $\tilde s(u) = s(r(u))$ of $U \triangleleft F \to U$ with (1) $\tilde s = s$ on $O$; (2) $R(r(u), \tilde s(u)) = s(r(u))$.

lean.statement: For a section $s$ of $K \to O$ ($(x, s(x)) \in K$ on $O$): $s(r(x)) = s(x)$ on $O$, and $\rho(r(u))s(r(u)) = s(r(u))$, $R(r(u), s(r(u))) = (r(u), s(r(u)))$ for $u \in U$. That $s \circ r$ is sc-smooth into $F^1$ is proved inside Theorem 3.1.18 (preprint 3.15).

diff: (2) is \"$R$ fixes the points of $K$\" and uses that an sc$^+$-section is a section. The sc$^+$ regularity of $\tilde s$ is supplied in the proof of Theorem 3.1.18 (preprint 3.15), where it is needed (Findings, Chapter 3, item 17).

items.title: Lemma 3.1.20 (preprint 3.17): fillers are stable under sc$^+$-sections

book.label: §3.1, Lemma 3.1.20 (preprint 3.17), p. 99 (preprint p. 72)
book.statement: If the sc-smooth section $f : O \to K$ has the filler $g$ and $s : O \to K$ is an sc$^+$-section, then $f + s$ has the filler $g + \tilde s$.

lean.statement: If $g$ is a filling of $\mathbf f$ (`IsFillingGerm`, V3.7) and $s$ is a section of $K \to O$, then $g + s \circ r$ is a filling of $\mathbf f + s$, with the same derivative family in (3): for $s$ sc-smooth on $U$ on the same germ (`IsFillingGerm.add_section`), and for $s$ an sc-smooth germ on $G \cap r^{-1}(G_s)$ (`IsFillingGerm.add_section_germ`); (3) because $[1 - \rho(r(y))](g + s \circ r)(y) = [1 - \rho(r(y))]g(y)$. For whole-chart fillers (`IsFillerOf`, no regularity of $g$) and any section $s$: `lemma_3_17`.

diff: The regularity of $g + \tilde s$ (“follow immediately”) is part of the conclusion: $s \circ r$ is a germ by the chain rule with the whole-chart $r$, and a sum of germs is a germ on the intersection (Findings, Chapter 3, items 270, 271, 273). Of $s$ only the sc-smoothness is used, not that it is sc$^+$.

**Germs.** Since the switch to the text’s germ reading (phase 2) the lemma is the text’s, for fillings that are germs, and proved in the project; the round-trip audit had found it true outside the project. The whole-chart `lemma_3_17` (fillers in the sense of `IsFillerOf`, the regularity left to Theorem 3.1.18 (preprint 3.15)) neither implies it nor follows from it (round-trip item V3.19; Findings, Chapter 3, items 220–221, 273). Hence “stronger” (formerly “restated”).

items.title: Definition 3.1.24 (preprint 3.21): good position

book.label: §3.1, Definition 3.1.24 (preprint 3.21), pp. 102–103 (preprint pp. 76–77)
book.statement: A finite-dimensional sc-subspace $N \subseteq E$ is in good position to the partial quadrant $C$ if $N \cap C$ has nonempty interior in $N$ and $N$ has an sc-complement $P$ (a good complement) with: for some $\varepsilon > 0$, $|p|_0 \le \varepsilon|n|_0$ implies ($n \in C \iff n + p \in C$). A merely topological complement is allowed for non-smooth $N$.

lean.statement: `IsGoodComplement E C N P`: $E_0 = N \oplus P$ algebraically and the $\varepsilon$-condition; `IsInGoodPosition E C N`: $N \cap C$ has nonempty interior in $N$ and $N$ has a good complement. $N$ finite-dimensional is a separate instance argument. Definition 3.1.24 (preprint 3.21) as written: `IsScGoodComplement` ($E = N \oplus P$ an sc-splitting, with the constant $\varepsilon$) and `IsInGoodPositionSc`; each implies the project's form. On a partial quadrant a smooth finite-dimensional $N$ in good position (algebraic complement) is in good position with an sc-complement, also inside any sc-subspace $T \supseteq N$; for smooth $N$ the text's good complements are the project's closed ones, and Definition 3.1.24 (preprint 3.21) as written is the project's good position together with $N \subseteq E_\infty$.

diff: Only the algebraic splitting is required: neither the sc-structure nor the closedness of $P$ enters Proposition 3.1.25 (preprint 3.22), Lemmas 3.5.9, 3.8.8 (preprint 3.45, 3.65) or Proposition 3.8.12 (preprint 3.69) (Findings, Chapter 3, item 19). Where closedness is needed (Lemma 3.6.9 (preprint 3.55), Definition 3.2.1 (preprint 3.25)) it is added there.
Typo preprint p. 77: \"finite dimensional sunspace\" *(book 2017: corrected, p. 69)*.

As a *conclusion* the algebraic form is weaker than the text's: an algebraic good complement need not be closed (round-trip item V3.20: $C = E_0$ infinite-dimensional, $P$ the kernel of a discontinuous functional; not in the project). The text's definition is therefore formalized as well, and on a partial quadrant the two agree for smooth $N$: a closed good complement of a smooth $N$ is an sc-complement (the projection along $N$ acts on every level), and a closed good complement always exists there (Findings, Chapter 3, items 210, 211). The theorems that conclude good position are given in the sc form in V3.94, V3.95. Updated in the third addendum of this page.

items.title: Proposition 3.1.25 (preprint 3.22): $N \cap C$ is a partial quadrant

book.label: §3.1, Proposition 3.1.25 (preprint 3.22), p. 103 (preprint p. 77) (proof §3.8.1, pp. 143–153 (preprint pp. 120–126))
book.statement: If the finite-dimensional sc-subspace $N$ is in good position to the partial quadrant $C$, then $N \cap C$ is a partial quadrant in $N$.

lean.statement: For $N$ finite-dimensional in good position to the partial quadrant $C$: $N \cap C$ is a partial quadrant in $N$ (constant sc-structure). The core: for continuous functionals $\ell_1, \dots, \ell_n$ jointly onto $\mathbb R^n$ with $C = \{\ell_i \ge 0\}$, a linear isomorphism $e : N \to \mathbb R^k \times N_0$ with $N \cap C = e^{-1}([0, \infty)^k \times N_0)$, $k = \dim N - \dim(N \cap W)$.

diff: The statement is the text's. The proof keeps the text's case distinction but replaces Lemmas 3.8.1–3.8.3 (preprint 3.62–3.64; Krein–Milman for cones, extreme-ray counts, cited from [21]) and 3.8.9–3.8.11 (preprint 3.66–3.68) by a segment argument and the surjectivity of $Q : N \to \mathbb R^\Sigma$ from Lemma 3.8.8 (preprint 3.65); the case $N \cap C = N$ is treated separately (Findings, Chapter 3, item 18).

items.title: Definition 3.2.1 (preprint 3.25): the $n$-dimensional tangent germ property

book.label: §3.2, Definition 3.2.1 (preprint 3.25), p. 104 (preprint p. 79)
book.statement: $M \subseteq X$ (tame) has the $n$-dimensional tangent germ property if $M \subseteq X_\infty$ and every $x \in M$ has a chart $\varphi : (U, x) \to (O, 0)$ onto a tame retract $(O, C, E)$, an $n$-dimensional smooth $N \subseteq E$ in good position to $C$ with good complement $Y$, $E = N \oplus Y$, a relatively open $V \ni 0$ in $N \cap C$ and a continuous $\delta : V \to Y$ with (i) $\varphi(M \cap U) = \{v + \delta(v)\}$, (ii) $\delta : \mathcal O(N \cap C, 0) \to (Y, 0)$ an sc$^\infty$-germ, $\delta(0) = 0$, $D\delta(0) = 0$.

lean.statement: `MPolyfold.TangentGermChart M x n`: the data of (2), with $Y$ **closed**, and (ii) read as `IsScInftyGermAt`: for every $m$ and $k$ a relatively open $V_{m,k} \ni 0$ in $N \cap C$ with $\delta(V_{m,k}) \subseteq E_m$ and $\delta : V_{m,k} \to E_m$ of class $C^k$. `MPolyfold.HasTangentGermProperty M n`: $M \subseteq X_\infty$ and the data at every point. Both other readings of \"sc$^\infty$-germ\" (one fixed germ; sc-smooth on $V$) imply this one.

diff: **Added hypothesis: the good complement $Y$ is closed**, needed for the projection $\pi : E \to N$ along $Y$ to be continuous (Findings, Chapter 3, item 81); the text's sc-complement is closed.

\"sc$^\infty$-germ\" is read with $k$-dependent neighbourhoods, the reading in which Theorem 3.5.6 (1) (preprint 3.43) is proved (V3.38) and the weakest of the three (Findings, Chapter 3, item 80); Corollary 3.3.7 (preprint 3.34) now also holds on one germ (V3.31, third addendum).

items.title: Proposition 3.2.2 (preprint 3.26): invariance of the tangent germ property

book.label: §3.2, Proposition 3.2.2 (preprint 3.26), p. 105 (preprint p. 80)
book.statement: For a pair $(X, M)$ with $X$ a tame M-polyfold, and an sc-diffeomorphism $\psi : X \to X'$ with $\psi(M) = M'$: $M'$ has the $n$-dimensional tangent germ property iff $M$ has it.

lean.statement: For an sc-diffeomorphism $\psi : X \to X'$ of M-polyfolds with inverse $\psi'$ (sc-smooth both ways on all of $X$, $X'$) and $\psi(M) = M'$: $M'$ has the $n$-dimensional tangent germ property iff $M$ has it. The data at $\psi(x)$ are the transported chart $\varphi \circ \psi^{-1}$ with the same $N$, $Y$, $V$, $\delta$; $\psi(M) \subseteq X'_\infty$ because sc-smooth maps preserve the levels.

diff: As in the text, for Definition 3.2.1 (preprint 3.25) as formalized (V3.22, $Y$ closed); the tameness of $X$ is not used (the chart models are tame retracts as part of the data).
The text's first sentence, that $X' = \psi(X)$ is tame, is not needed here; that tameness is carried by sc-diffeomorphisms is V3.71.

items.title: Theorem 3.2.3 (preprint 3.27): subsets with the tangent germ property are sub-M-polyfolds

book.label: §3.2, Theorem 3.2.3 (preprint 3.27), p. 106 (preprint p. 81) (proof pp. 106–109 (preprint pp. 81–84))
book.statement: If $X$ is a tame M-polyfold and $M \subseteq X$ has the $n$-dimensional tangent germ property, then (1) $M$ is a sub-M-polyfold whose induced structure is tame and sc-smoothly equivalent to a smooth manifold with boundary with corners; (2) with the data of Definition 3.2.1 (preprint 3.25), $y \mapsto \pi \circ \varphi(y)$ is a smooth chart of $M$ around $x$.

lean.statement: Let $M \ne \emptyset$ have at every point data of Definition 3.2.1 (preprint 3.25) satisfying `IsRegular`: (a) $\delta$ is sc-smooth on $V$ (set sense), (b) $\pi(O) \subseteq C$. Then $M$ is a sub-M-polyfold (retraction $s = \varphi^{-1} \circ t \circ \varphi$, $t(v + w) = v + \delta(v)$); its induced structure is tame and has an equivalent atlas of $n$-dimensional corner charts; every $y \mapsto \pi\varphi(y)$ is a chart of the induced structure, modelled on $(V, N \cap C, N)$; and $d_M(y) = d_{N \cap C}(\pi\varphi(y))$.

diff: **Two added hypotheses (`IsRegular`), each with a counterexample to the text's step.** (a) \"$\delta$ is an sc$^\infty$-germ near every $v_0 \in V$\" needs $\delta$ differentiable at $v_0$: a smooth curve in $\mathbb R^2$ with a vertical tangent at $(2, 4)$, written over the $x$-axis, satisfies Definition 3.2.1 (preprint 3.25) at $0$ with $\delta$ not differentiable at $2$, and the chart $\pi\varphi$ is then not smoothly compatible (Findings, Chapter 3, item 82). (b) \"$\Sigma = \{v + y \in C\}$ is relatively open in $C$\" is false for $C = [0, \infty)^3$, $N = \mathbb R(1, 1, 1)$, $Y = \{x + y - z = 0\}$ (item 83).

Tameness of $X$ is not used (only that the chart models are tame retracts). \"Manifold with boundary with corners\" (Chapter 4) is `IsManifoldWithCorners`: an equivalent atlas of charts on relatively open subsets of $n$-dimensional partial quadrants. The relation $d_{N \cap C}(v) = d_X(y)$ via Lemma 3.8.13 (preprint 3.70) is proved in the model $\mathbb R^n \oplus W$ only (item 84).

For the solution set of an sc-Fredholm section both conditions are theorems: (a) by re-centring (V3.73, V3.74), (b) by the choice of the good complement (V3.75, V3.77); read off the statement of V3.74, (a) follows from (b) after shrinking the data for any set with the tangent germ property. With a dimension that may vary from point to point: V3.72.

items.title: Definition 3.3.1 (preprint 3.28): sc$^0$-contraction germs and their working form

book.label: §3.3, Definition 3.3.1 (preprint 3.28), p. 109 (preprint p. 85)
book.statement: An sc$^0$-germ $f : \mathcal O(\widetilde C \oplus W, 0) \to (W, 0)$ is an sc$^0$-contraction germ if $f(a, w) = w - B(a, w)$ and for every $\varepsilon > 0$, $m \ge 0$, $|B(a, w) - B(a, w')|_m \le \varepsilon|w - w'|_m$ for $(a, w), (a, w')$ on level $m$ sufficiently close to $(0, 0)$.

lean.statement: `IsSc0ContractionGerm C̃ G B`: $B$ an sc$^0$-germ on $G$, $B(0, 0) = 0$, and for every $\varepsilon$, $m$ an $r > 0$ with the estimate for $a \in \widetilde C$, $|a| < r$, $|w|_m, |w'|_m < r$, these points lying in $U_m$. The working form `ContractionGerm`: the same data with explicit regions $N(m) \subseteq P$ open, $K(m) \subseteq O(m) \subseteq W_m$ ($K$ closed, $O$ open) on which $B_m(a, \cdot)$ is a $\tfrac12$-contraction ($O$) mapping $K$ into itself; every contraction germ has one.

diff: The balls of the definition cannot express the regions of $f^{(1)}$ in Lemma 3.3.4 (preprint 3.31), which are unbounded in the tangent directions; the working form carries explicit regions (Findings, Chapter 3, items 3, 7).
§3.3 is proved for any convex $\widetilde C \ni 0$ with nonempty interior in a finite-dimensional $P$ (item 9).

items.title: Theorem 3.3.2 (preprint 3.29): existence of the solution germ

book.label: §3.3, Theorem 3.3.2 (preprint 3.29), p. 110 (preprint p. 86)
book.statement: An sc$^0$-contraction germ $f : \mathcal O(\widetilde C \oplus W, 0) \to (W, 0)$ admits a uniquely determined sc$^0$-solution germ $\delta : \mathcal O(\widetilde C, 0) \to (W, 0)$ with $f(a, \delta(a)) = 0$; proof by \"the parametrized version of Banach's fixed point theorem\".

lean.statement: In the working form, $\delta$ (the level-$0$ fixed point) is an sc$^0$-germ on $V_m = N(m) \cap \widetilde C$ with $\delta(0) = 0$, $(a, \delta_m(a)) \in U_m$ and $B(a, \delta(a)) = \delta(a)$, and every solution $w \in O(0)$ of $w = B(a, w)$, $a \in V_0$, equals $\delta(a)$. From Definition 3.3.1 (preprint 3.28) directly: the same with uniqueness in a ball. The parametrized fixed point theorem: the fixed point of a family of $\tfrac12$-contractions of a closed set, continuous in the parameter pointwise, is continuous in the parameter.

diff: \"Uniquely determined\" holds in the contraction region $O(0)$ (the text's Remark 3.3.8 (preprint 3.36): $|w|_0 \le \tau_0$).

The parametrized Banach fixed point theorem, which the text invokes without statement, is proved (Mathlib has the theorem without the parameter). Typo preprint p. 85: \"$\delta_1 : V_1 \to W_1$ satisfying $\delta(0) = 0$\" for $\delta_1(0) = 0$ *(book 2017: unchanged, p. 77)*.

items.title: Theorem 3.3.3 (preprint 3.30): the solution germ is sc$^1$

book.label: §3.3, Theorem 3.3.3 (preprint 3.30), p. 110 (preprint p. 86) (cited from [21, Theorem 2.3], no proof)
book.statement: If the sc$^0$-contraction germ $f : \mathcal O(\widetilde C \oplus W, 0) \to (W, 0)$ is of class sc$^1$, its solution germ $\delta$ is of class sc$^1$.

lean.statement: If $B$ is an sc$^1$-germ, then $\delta$ is a solution germ and an sc$^1$-germ **on the re-indexed germ** $V_m = N(m+1) \cap \widetilde C$, with derivative $D\delta(a) = (1 - D_2B(a, \delta(a)))^{-1}D_1B(a, \delta(a))$.

chips: sc¹ on the germ shifted by one level
diff: The text gives no proof. The formal proof needs $(a_0, \delta(a_0)) \in U_2$ (level-$1$ operators, so that the increment $A h$ lies in $W_1$), hence holds on the germ shifted by one level; legitimate as a germ only because $\widetilde C$ is finite-dimensional (Findings, Chapter 3, item 1). In the text's \"up to shrinking\" reading this is \"$\delta$ is sc$^1$\".

items.title: Lemma 3.3.4 (preprint 3.31): the contraction germ $f^{(1)}$

book.label: §3.3, Lemma 3.3.4 (preprint 3.31), pp. 111 ff. (preprint pp. 86–87)
book.statement: If $f = w - B(a, w)$ is an sc$^0$-contraction germ of class sc$^k$, $k \ge 1$, with solution germ $\delta$ of class sc$^j$, then $f^{(1)}(v, b, u, w) = (u - B(v, u), w - DB(v, \delta(v))(b, w))$ is an sc$^0$-contraction germ of class sc$^{\min(k-1, j)}$ with solution germ $T\delta$ (\"from the uniqueness\").

lean.statement: If $B$ is sc$^{k+1}$ and $\delta$ is sc$^j$ on $\mathrm{germ}(s) = (N(m+s) \cap \widetilde C)_m$, then $f^{(1)}$, in working form with parameter space $P \times P \supseteq \widetilde C \times P$, fibre $TW$ and regions $N(m+2+s) \times P$, $O(m+1) \times W_m$, $K(m+1) \times W_m$, is a contraction germ of class sc$^{\min(k, j)}$ whose solution germ is $T\delta(v, b) = (\delta(v), D\delta(v)b)$ on $(N(2+s) \cap \widetilde C) \times P$. Its map is $(\mathrm{pr}_1 \circ TB \circ \sigma, \mathrm{pr}_2 \circ TB \circ \Gamma)$ with $\sigma$ a reshuffle and $\Gamma(v, b, u, w) = ((v, \delta(v)), (b, w))$. If the working form also satisfies Definition 3.3.1 (preprint 3.28) (as the one built from an sc$^0$-contraction germ does) and $B$ is sc$^1$, then $f^{(1)}$ is an sc$^0$-contraction germ in the sense of Definition 3.3.1 (preprint 3.28) on its germ, for every $s$: an $\varepsilon$-contraction near $0$ for every $\varepsilon > 0$ on every level.

diff: Uniqueness holds only in the contraction region, which must contain $T\delta(v, b)$ for every $b$: the regions are unbounded in $b$, $w$ (Findings, Chapter 3, item 3). \"As one verifies by comparing $Tf$ with $f^{(1)}$\" is the chain rule for germs with the shifted solution germ $v \mapsto \delta(v) \in W_1$ (Proposition 1.2.2 (preprint 1.17) for germs, item 4). The parameter region $N(2+s)$ comes from $D\delta(v)$ needing $v \in N(2)$.

The text's “$f^{(1)}$ is an sc$^0$-contraction germ” in the sense of Definition 3.3.1 (preprint 3.28) is proved separately (`isSc0ContractionGerm_next`): on level $m$ its first component is Definition 3.3.1 (preprint 3.28) for $B$ on level $m + 1$, its second needs Lemma 3.1.9 (preprint 3.9) on level $m$ with any $\varepsilon$ (V3.11). The working form records only a $\tfrac12$-contraction on the explicit regions, which is all the proof of Theorem 3.3.6 (preprint 3.33) uses (Findings, Chapter 3, item 252). Updated in the third addendum of this page.

items.title: Lemma 3.3.5 (preprint 3.32): the iterated contraction germs

book.label: §3.3, Lemma 3.3.5 (preprint 3.32), p. 111 (preprint p. 87)
book.statement: Given an sc$^0$-contraction germ $f$ of class sc$^k$ and a solution germ $\delta$ of class sc$^j$, $j \le k$, there is an sc$^0$-contraction germ $f^{(j)}$ of class sc$^{\min(k-j, 1)}$ with solution germ $T^j\delta$.

lean.statement: As one induction over all contraction germs (any finite-dimensional parameter space): if $B$ is sc$^k$ and $j \le k$, the solution germ $\delta$ is an sc$^j$-germ on $\mathrm{germ}(s)$ for some $s$. The step $j \to j+1$: $\delta$ sc$^j$, so $f^{(1)}$ is sc$^j$, so $T\delta$ is sc$^j$ (the induction hypothesis for $f^{(1)}$), and $\delta$ is sc$^1$ (Theorem 3.3.3 (preprint 3.30)); then $\delta$ is sc$^{j+1}$ on $\mathrm{germ}(s + s' + 1)$.

diff: The iterated germs $f^{(j)}$ are not constructed; the content of the lemma (its step $j \to j+1$) is the induction step (Findings, Chapter 3, item 5).

items.title: Theorem 3.3.6 (preprint 3.33): the germ implicit function theorem

book.label: §3.3, Theorem 3.3.6 (preprint 3.33), p. 112 (preprint p. 88)
book.statement: If $f : \mathcal O(\widetilde C \oplus W, 0) \to (W, 0)$ is an sc$^0$-contraction germ of class sc$^k$, its solution germ $\delta$, $f(v, \delta(v)) = 0$, is of class sc$^k$.

lean.statement: If $B$ is an sc$^k$-germ, there is $s$ such that $\delta$ is a solution germ and an sc$^k$-germ **on the shrunken germ** $\mathrm{germ}(s) = (N(m+s) \cap \widetilde C)_m$; the proof gives $s = 2^k - 1$. The same from Definition 3.3.1 (preprint 3.28) with balls.

chips: sc^k on a germ shrunk by $2^k - 1$
diff: **Proved with the text's hypotheses.** The germ shrinks with $k$: each induction step uses the previous stage twice, so $s_{j+1} = 2s_j + 1$ (Findings, Chapter 3, item 2). In the text's reading, where germs are up to shrinking, this is the theorem; with a germ as a fixed sequence of sets the conclusion holds on $\mathrm{germ}(2^k - 1)$, not on the germ of construction.

The statement keeps \"there is $s$\"; $s = 2^k - 1$ is read off the proof. Whether the shrinking is intrinsic is not decided: in the toy model of the exposition the solution germ is sc-smooth on the original germ.

items.title: Corollary 3.3.7 (preprint 3.34): $C^k$ on $k$-dependent neighbourhoods

book.label: §3.3, Corollary 3.3.7 (preprint 3.34), p. 113 (preprint p. 88)
book.statement: If the sc$^0$-contraction germ $f$ is sc-smooth, then for all $m, k \ge 0$ there is a relatively open $V_{m,k} \ni 0$ in $\widetilde C$ with (1) $\delta(V_{m,k}) \subseteq W_m$, (2) $\delta : V_{m,k} \to W_m$ of class $C^k$. In particular $\delta$ is sc-smooth at the smooth point $0$.

lean.statement: If $B$ is an sc-smooth germ, then for every $m$ and $k$ there is a relatively open $V \ni 0$ in $\widetilde C$ (namely $N(m+k+s) \cap \widetilde C$) with $\delta(V) \subseteq W_m$ and the level-$m$ map of $\delta$ of class $C^k$ on $V$. The last sentence on one germ: the solution germ is an sc-smooth germ (sc$^k$ for every $k$ on the same sequence of sets) on a diagonal germ $V_m = N(m + t_m) \cap \widetilde C$, $t_m = \sum_{j \le m} s_j$, and a solution germ there.

diff: As in the text, with $V_{m,k}$ depending on $k$. The last sentence holds on one germ: sc$^j$ involves only the levels $\ge j$ of a germ (`isSckGerm_of_levels`), so the $k$-dependent germs $\mathrm{germ}(s_k)$ of Theorem 3.3.6 (preprint 3.33) can be replaced by one diagonal germ, which shrinks fast with the level ($t_m = 2^{m+1} - m - 2$ for $s_k = 2^k - 1$) but is a germ of neighbourhoods (Findings, Chapter 3, item 250; formerly “in this sense only”, updated in the third addendum of this page). The citation \"Proposition 3.40\" should be Theorem 3.5.1 (preprint 3.40), and it is not needed *(book 2017: unchanged, renumbered: "Proposition 3.11" for Theorem 3.11, p. 79)* (Findings, Chapter 3, item 8).

items.title: Theorem 3.35 (preprint; not in the 2021 edition): the germ implicit function theorem on a partial quadrant

book.label: §3.3, Theorem 3.35 (preprint), preprint p. 89
book.statement: Let $\widetilde C$ be a finite-dimensional partial quadrant in $\mathbb R^n$. An sc$^0$-contraction germ of class sc$^k$ has a solution germ of class sc$^k$; if $f$ is sc-smooth so is its solution germ.

lean.statement: For $\widetilde C$ a partial quadrant in a finite-dimensional $P$: if $B$ is sc$^k$ there is $s$ with $\delta$ sc$^k$ on $\mathrm{germ}(s)$; if $B$ is sc-smooth, $\delta$ is an sc-smooth germ (sc$^k$ for every $k$) on **one** germ $N(m + t_m) \cap \widetilde C$ (earlier form: for every $k$ an $s$ with $\delta$ sc$^k$ on $\mathrm{germ}(s)$). In the text's form: for an sc$^0$-contraction germ $f = w - B(a, w)$ of Definition 3.3.1 (preprint 3.28) on a quadrant-like $\widetilde C$ and **any** representative $(V, \delta)$ of its solution germ ($\delta$ sc$^0$, $\delta(0) = 0$, $f(a, \delta(a)) = 0$ on $V_0$): if $f$ is sc$^k$, $\delta$ is sc$^k$ on a germ $V' \subseteq V$; if $f$ is sc-smooth, $\delta$ is an sc-smooth germ on one germ $V' \subseteq V$.

diff: The last sentence is proved as `IsScSmoothGerm` on one germ (the diagonal germ of V3.31); before the third addendum of this page only for every $k$ on a germ depending on $k$ (Findings, Chapter 3, items 2, 250).

In the text's form the hypotheses are on $f$ ($f$ is sc$^k$ iff $B$ is, `isSckGerm_contractionMap_iff`) and any representative of the solution germ is allowed (it agrees with the constructed one near $0$, by the uniqueness of Theorem 3.3.2 (preprint 3.29)); the conclusion holds on a smaller germ $V' \subseteq V$, as for Theorem 3.3.6 (preprint 3.33) (V3.30), and $\mathbb R^n$ is generalized to a quadrant-like $\widetilde C$ in a finite-dimensional $P$ (Findings, Chapter 3, item 251). Updated in the third addendum of this page.

items.title: Definition 3.4.1 (preprint 3.37): the basic class

book.label: §3.4, Definition 3.4.1 (preprint 3.37), p. 114 (preprint p. 90)
book.statement: A basic germ $f : \mathcal O([0, \infty)^k \oplus \mathbb R^{n-k} \oplus W, 0) \to (\mathbb R^N \oplus W, 0)$ is an sc-smooth germ such that $P_W \circ f$ is an sc$^0$-contraction germ; $\mathfrak C_{\mathrm{basic}}$ is the class of basic germs.

lean.statement: Definition 3.1.7 (preprint 3.7) restated: `IsBasicGerm` (V3.10).

diff: Same notion as Definition 3.1.7 (preprint 3.7).

items.title: Theorem 3.4.2 (preprint 3.38): weak stability of basic germs

book.label: §3.4, Theorem 3.4.2 (preprint 3.38), p. 114 (preprint p. 90) (proof pp. 113–117 (preprint pp. 90–93))
book.statement: For a basic germ $f$ and the principal part $s$ of an sc$^+$-section with $s(0) = 0$ there is a strong bundle isomorphism $\Phi : U \triangleleft (\mathbb R^N \oplus W) \to U' \triangleleft (\mathbb R^{N'} \oplus W')$ covering an sc-diffeomorphism $\varphi$ such that $(\Phi_*(f + s))^1$ (levels raised by one) is a basic germ; $n - N = n' - N'$.

lean.statement: Given $f$ basic with contraction $B$ and the data `StabilityData` (the $W$-component $s$ of the sc$^+$-germ, $s(0) = 0$, and an sc-Fredholm splitting $W = C \oplus X = R \oplus Z$ of $1 + D_2s(0)$, which exists by Proposition 1.1.11 (preprint 1.10)): with the **linear** base change $\psi(a, w) = ((a, (1 - P_1)w), P_1w)$ and fibre change $\Psi(q, w) = ((q, (1 - P_2)w), L^{-1}P_2w)$, the germ $(\Phi_*(f + s))^1 = \Psi \circ (f + s)^1 \circ \psi^{-1}$ on $\psi(U_{m+1})$ is a basic germ with contraction $\hat B = L^{-1}P_2(B - S)$; zeros correspond under $\psi$; and $\dim C = \dim Z$.

diff: The coordinate change is linear, so a pair of sc-isomorphisms replaces a general strong bundle isomorphism; the text's $\tau : Z \to C$ is not applied (new target $(Q \oplus Z) \oplus X^1$). The index raise is a change of sc-structure (Proposition 1.2.2 (preprint 1.17) for germs) (Findings, Chapter 3, items 60–61).

\"$S$ is an arbitrarily small contraction on every level $m \ge 1$\" needs the operator-norm continuity of the derivative of $s$ on level $m + 1$ and the mean value inequality (item 62). Only the $W$-component of $s$ enters; $B$ is used only through Definition 3.1.7 (preprint 3.7) (item 63).
The linear coordinate change is a strong bundle isomorphism of the index-raised structures (`StabilityData.linIso_isStrongBundleIso`, V3.76).

items.title: Theorem 3.5.1 (preprint 3.40): local regularity and compactness

book.label: §3.5, Theorem 3.5.1 (preprint 3.40), p. 118 (preprint p. 94) (proof pp. 118–123 (preprint pp. 95–98))
book.statement: Let $f = h + s : U \to \mathbb R^N \oplus W$, $h$ a basic germ, $s$ an sc$^+$-germ with $s(0) = 0$, $S = \{f = 0\}$. There are relatively open neighbourhoods $U \supset O(0) \supset O(1) \supset \cdots$ of $0$ on level $0$ with $\mathrm{cl}_{C_0}(S \cap O(m)) \subseteq C_m$.

lean.statement: Let $B$ be an sc$^0$-contraction germ on $\widetilde C \oplus W$ with **$\widetilde C$ closed**, $\mathbf s$ sc$^0$ into $W^1$ with $\mathbf s(0) = 0$, and $S$ any set of solutions of $w = B(a, w) - \mathbf s(a, w)$ in $U_0$. There are nested open $O(i) \ni 0$ in $E_0$ with $\mathrm{cl}_{E_0}(S \cap O(i)) = \iota_i(K_i)$ for compact $K_i \subseteq E_i$; in particular $\mathrm{cl}(S \cap O(i)) \subseteq E_i$. For a basic germ plus an sc$^+$-germ this gives the local Theorem 3.1.13 (preprint 3.12).

diff: Stronger: the closures are compact in $E_i$, which Theorem 3.1.13 (preprint 3.12) needs and Theorem 3.5.1 (preprint 3.40) does not state (Findings, Chapter 3, item 12). Weaker hypotheses: of $f$ only the $W$-component, with $B$ sc$^0$ and the contraction estimate, and $\mathbf s$ sc$^0$ into $W^1$ (item 14).

**$\widetilde C$ closed** is a hypothesis because the theorem is proved for convex $\widetilde C$; it holds for partial quadrants. The induction left to the reader needs existence, bound and continuity of the lifts together (item 13); the $O(i)$ are one level ahead of the text's.

items.title: Corollary 3.5.3 (preprint 3.41): the linearization at nearby solutions

book.label: §3.5, Corollary 3.5.3 (preprint 3.41), p. 122 (preprint p. 98) (proof pp. 121–125 (preprint pp. 98–100))
book.statement: For $f = h + s : U \to \mathbb R^N \oplus W$, $h$ basic, $s$ an sc$^+$-map, $s(0) = 0$, $Df(0)$ surjective: there is $U' \subseteq U$ relatively open on level $0$ such that (1) solutions in $U'$ are on level $1$; (2) at such solutions $Df(a, w) : E \to F$ is a surjective Fredholm operator of index $n - N$.

lean.statement: For the data of Theorem 3.4.2 (preprint 3.38) ($f := h$ basic, $s$ the $W$-component of the sc$^+$-germ) with $D(h + s)(0)$ surjective: there is $r > 0$ such that every zero $x$ of $h + s$ in $U_0$ with $|x|_0 < r$ is $\iota(x_1)$ with $x_1 \in U_1$, and $D(h + s)(x_1) : E_0 \to F_0$ is a surjective Fredholm operator of index $\dim P - \dim Q$.

diff: The $\mathbb R^N$-component of the sc$^+$-map is absorbed into $h$ (as in Theorem 3.6.8 (preprint 3.54), Findings item 85). The Fredholm property with index holds at every $x \in U_1$ small on level $1$, not only at solutions; $Df(x) = Df(0) + S(x) + K(x)$ with $\|S(x)\| \le \varepsilon$ and $K(x)$ compact; surjectivity from $\dim\ker \le n - N = \mathrm{ind}$; the detour through level $2$ is not needed (item 71).

items.title: Lemma 3.5.5 (preprint 3.42): solutions of the push-forward are on level 1

book.label: §3.5, Lemma 3.5.5 (preprint 3.42), p. 126 (preprint p. 101)
book.statement: (In the setting after Theorem 3.4.2 (preprint 3.38), $g = \Phi_*f$, $\delta$ the solution germ of $P' \circ g^1$.) There are $\varepsilon'_0, \tau'_0$ such that a solution $(a', w')$ of $g = 0$ with $|a'|_0 \le \varepsilon'_0$, $|w'|_0 \le \tau'_0$ has $w' = \delta(a')$, and $|\delta(a')|_0 \le \tau'_0$ if $|a'|_0 \le \varepsilon'_0$.

lean.statement: For every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $r > 0$ such that every zero $x'$ of $g = \Phi_*(f + s)$ in $\psi(U)$ with $|x'|_0 < r$ has its $X$-component on level $1$ with $|\cdot|_1 < \varepsilon$.

diff: The formal statement is the regularity Theorem 3.5.6's (preprint 3.43) proof uses (solutions near $0$ lie on level $1$ and are small there), proved from the lifts of Theorem 3.5.1 (preprint 3.40) and the linearity of $\psi$; the identification $w' = \delta(a')$ is made inside Theorem 3.5.6 (preprint 3.43) (Findings, Chapter 3, item 65).

items.title: Theorem 3.5.6 (preprint 3.43): local germ-solvability I

book.label: §3.5, Theorem 3.5.6 (preprint 3.43), p. 126 (preprint p. 102) (proof pp. 126–131 (preprint pp. 102–106))
book.statement: Let $f = h + s$ with $Df(0)$ surjective and $K = \ker Df(0)$ in good position to $C$, $g = \Phi_*(f)$. Then $K' = \ker Dg(0)$ is in good position to $C'$, there are a good complement $Y'$ and a $C^1$ map $\tau : V \to Y'_1$, $V$ relatively open in $K' \cap C'$, with (1) $\tau$ an sc-smooth germ; (2) $\tau(0) = 0$, $D\tau(0) = 0$; (3) after shrinking $U$, $\varphi(\{f = 0\}) = \{g = 0\} = \{y + \tau(y) \mid y \in V\}$.

lean.statement: For an sc-smooth germ $g$ with $g(0) = 0$ whose index-raised germ $g^1$ is basic (`ShiftedBasicData`), $\widetilde C$ a partial quadrant, $Dg(0)$ onto, $K' = \ker Dg(0)$ in good position, and the regularity hypothesis of Lemma 3.5.5 (preprint 3.42): there are a good complement $Y = Z \oplus W$, $V$ relatively open in $K' \cap C'$ and $\tau : V \to Y$ of class $C^1$ with values on level $1$, $\tau(0) = 0$, $D\tau(0) = 0$, every $y + \tau(y)$ a zero in $U$, every zero in $U$ near $0$ of this form; and (1) for every $k \ge 1$ a relatively open $V_k \subseteq V$ containing $0$ and a $C^k$ map $\tau_k : V_k \to E_k$ with $\iota_k\tau_k = \tau$ on $V_k$.

diff: (1), \"$\tau$ is an sc-smooth germ\", is proved level-wise with $k$-dependent neighbourhoods (the reading of V3.22 and Corollary 3.3.7 (preprint 3.34)): $C^k$ into $E_k$ on $V_k$. The proof applies Theorem 3.8.22 (preprint 3.78) to $H$ at regularity $k$ and identifies its solution with the $C^1$ one by the uniqueness clause, which the text does not discuss (Findings, Chapter 3, item 70). `theorem_3_43` is the statement without (1). Lemma 3.5.5 (preprint 3.42) enters as the explicit hypothesis `hreg`, proved for the push-forward of Theorem 3.4.2 (preprint 3.38) in V3.37 (item 65).

A gap in the text's proof of (3) is filled: the $\widetilde K$-component of a solution lies in $\widetilde C$, because $|z| \le \varepsilon|k|$ near $0$ (item 66). $H$ is $C^j$ near $0$ by Corollary 3.3.7 (preprint 3.34) for $g^1$ and Proposition 1.2.3 (preprint 1.18) for germs (item 67).
With the good complement closed and its projection onto $K'$ mapping $\widetilde C \oplus W$ into itself: V3.77.

items.title: Lemma 3.5.8 (preprint 3.44): the kernel of $Dg(0)$ is a graph

book.label: §3.5, Lemma 3.5.8 (preprint 3.44), p. 127 (preprint p. 103)
book.statement: The map $\alpha \mapsto (\alpha, D\delta(0)\alpha)$ induces a linear isomorphism $\widetilde K = \ker DH(0) \to \ker Dg(0) = K'$, $H(a) = (1 - P') \circ g(a, \delta(a))$.

items.title: Lemma 3.5.9 (preprint 3.45): good position under linear isomorphisms

book.label: §3.5, Lemma 3.5.9 (preprint 3.45), p. 128 (preprint p. 104)
book.statement: The complement $(K')^\perp = T\varphi(0)(K^\perp)$ is a good complement of $K' = T\varphi(0)K$ in $E'$.

items.title: Lemma 3.5.10 (preprint 3.46): good position of $\ker DH(0)$

book.label: §3.5, Lemma 3.5.10 (preprint 3.46), p. 129 (preprint p. 104) (proof §3.8.3 (preprint §3.8.2), pp. 155–161 (preprint pp. 129–132))

items.title: Theorem 3.5.11 (preprint Corollary 3.47): local germ-solvability for $f + s$

book.label: §3.5, Theorem 3.5.11 (preprint Corollary 3.47), p. 131 (preprint p. 106) (proof pp. 130–134 (preprint pp. 106–108))
book.statement: Under the hypotheses of Theorem 3.5.6 (preprint 3.43) there are a good complement $Y$ of $K$ and a $C^1$ map $\sigma : V \to Y_1$, $V$ relatively open in $K \cap C$, with (1) $\sigma$ an sc-smooth germ; (2) $\sigma(0) = 0$, $D\sigma(0) = 0$; (3) $\{x \in U \mid f(x) = 0\} = \{v + \sigma(v) \mid v \in V\}$ after shrinking $U$.

items.title: Definitions 3.6.3 and 3.6.4 (preprint 3.50 and 3.51): sc-Fredholm germs and sections of a tame strong bundle (restated)

All four in the text’s germ reading (V3.13); the whole-chart forms are `…WholeChart`.

**Germs.** Since the switch to the text’s germ reading (phase 2) the four notions take the filling and the sc$^+$-section as germs whose levels may shrink with $m$ (`IsFillingGerm`, `IsScPlusGerm`); the earlier whole-chart forms (`IsScFredholmGermTameWholeChart`, …), which imply them (round-trip item V3.45), are kept.
